extracted.intended_audience: research mathematicians (especially algebraic combinatorics and theoretical computer science), graduate students and interested mathematically-literate readers
extracted.subtask_description: Advice and normative claims about doing mathematical research (how to form and test beliefs, computational experimentation, exposition, and classificatory notions for counting functions) with emphasis on combinatorics and complexity-theoretic viewpoints. Includes domain definitions (complete/concise functions) and recommendations about publication, pedagogy, and professional behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accept foundational assumptions pragmatically
rubrics_metrics.description: Faith is the foundation of it all. You really can’t do math without foundations. For example, it’s perfectly fine to have a paper in algebra using the Axiom of Choice (AC) while in another in descriptive set theory, where you go out of your way to avoid AC.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not overthink foundational consistency (e.g., consistency of PA); adopt a 'multifaith personality' where different papers/areas may use different foundational assumptions as appropriate to the problem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Question and revise beliefs about conjectures
rubrics_metrics.description: Ideally, you should question your beliefs whenever possible. If you are thinking about a conjecture, are you sure you believe in it? Maybe you should try to disprove it instead? It’s ok to change your mind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Actively try both directions (prove and disprove); be willing to change beliefs in light of evidence (examples: Riemann Hypothesis, Goldbach, abc conjecture, Lyusternik–Schnirelmann theorem).

rubrics_metrics.name: Differentiate core beliefs and peripheral confidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Different beliefs usually have different levels of confidence. Some beliefs are core and people rarely change their mind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize which beliefs are core (hard to change) versus malleable; be explicit about confidence levels when reasoning or using conjectures as assumptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Translate beliefs into action (prove something) and update with evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: If you have a lot of beliefs that doesn’t make you smart. That makes you opinionated. To be considered smart you need to act on your beliefs and actually prove something. To be considered wise you need the ability to learn to adjust your belief system to avoid contradictions with your other beliefs as new evidence emerges.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer doing research that tests beliefs; avoid mere armchair opinion—turn beliefs into theorems, counterexamples, or concrete experiments and revise beliefs when results contradict them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Professional research is communal and role-based
rubrics_metrics.description: In mathematics, to practice an organized religion is to be professional, when you get paid for doing research. The process is fundamentally communal involving many people playing different roles (researcher, editor, referee, publisher, colleagues writing letters, students reading and extending work).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value community roles; understand that research becomes valuable in the context of a community (talks, seminars, students, refereeing, editorial processes).

rubrics_metrics.name: Value and convey 'miracles' (surprising mathematical insights)
rubrics_metrics.description: Miracles are the most delightful things that ever happen to you when learning or when doing mathematical research. You have to train yourself to see the miracles for what they are, rather than for what they now appear to be when textbook packages them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cultivate an appreciation for surprising constructions (e.g., RSK correspondence); teach and present results in ways that convey the initial 'miracle' to students and readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be willing to look for counterexamples; actively test widely-believed conjectures
rubrics_metrics.description: Why look for a counterexample if the conjecture is so obviously true? Well, because you always should. For any conjecture. Especially if everyone else is so sure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pursue counterexamples through experiments, thought, and collaboration; expect resistance but consider potential high impact (example: disproof of the Bunkbed Conjecture).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use computational experiments carefully; design good experiments and make work reproducible
rubrics_metrics.description: Please do try computer experiments for whatever you are working on. Make an effort to think it through and design a good experiment. Work hard to test as much as your computer technology allows. If you need some computing power, ask around. Make your code and work notes publicly available.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Share code and notes (GitHub, arXiv), attempt replication, and document experimental methodology; report negative results and failed experiments as they are valuable 'work product'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monte Carlo evidence is limited; formal proofs preferred for publication
rubrics_metrics.description: Since analyzing all of 2^m subgraphs is not feasible, our Monte Carlo simulations could only confirm the desired inequality with high probability. While this probability could be amplified by repeated testing, one could never formally disprove the bunkbed conjecture this way. Most journals would refuse to even consider a 'five sigma counterexample'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat high-confidence probabilistic/computational evidence as useful but insufficient for formal mathematical claims; strive for combinatorial/formal arguments when possible or clearly state conditional/probabilistic status.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anticipate reputational and career consequences of contrarian positions
rubrics_metrics.description: Breaking with conventional wisdom is a long and occasionally painful process. Worse, being a contrarian gives you a bad rap as you often get confused with being nihilistic. PhD students need jobs in reality, not in theory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be strategic when publicizing controversial results; mentor junior collaborators about career risks; document and publish work even if journals are reluctant (use arXiv).

rubrics_metrics.name: Combinatorial interpretation as a computational notion (#P perspective)
rubrics_metrics.description: The idea that a 'combinatorial interpretation' is simply a function in #P. Thinking of a 'closed formula' for a combinatorial counting function as algorithm for computing the function.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating whether a counting function has a combinatorial interpretation, adopt computational-complexity criteria (is it in #P? is positivity decidable?), and view closed forms as algorithms (analysis-of-algorithms viewpoint).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition: Complete and almost complete functions
rubrics_metrics.description: We say that f is complete if f(A)=N. Similarly f is almost complete if f(A) contains all sufficiently large integers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these notions to classify counting functions; examples given: number of perfect matchings (complete), number of domino tilings (complete), number of spanning trees (almost complete for n-cycles).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition: Concise function (size vs. value tradeoff)
rubrics_metrics.description: Let f be an almost complete function. We say that f is concise if for all large enough k, there exist an element a in A_n such that f(a)=k and n < C (log k)^c, for some C, c>0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conciseness captures 'small descriptions' producing large counts; explicit constructions (e.g., Brualdi–Newman for perfect matchings, domino-tiling gadgets) are central. Distinguish concise from merely complete/almost-complete by quantitative object-size bounds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity and audience-appropriate exposition in talks and papers
rubrics_metrics.description: Presentations are often shockingly bad when the lecturer reads his paper in a monotone, making the talk tedious and incomprehensible. Speakers should train and tailor their talks to the audience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not read papers verbatim in talks; prepare talks for the intended audience, aim for clear exposition, consider recording and online availability, and provide accessible materials for later viewing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer online dissemination and recorded talks to increase accessibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Stop having [large congresses] in the current form. All talks can be moved online so that everyone can watch them either as they happen, or later on YouTube. Spread online lectures across time zones so that people from different countries can participate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Record and post talks, reduce unnecessary travel/CO2, and use online platforms to broaden access and permit asynchronous viewing (x1.5 speed, segmented lectures).
